hep-statistics skill rules referred to for judging multiple-testing and selection-adjusted inference
answers.reasoning: Most of the quantitative content checks out. The rule of three (-ln 0.05 = 2.996), 1-0.95^20 = 0.6415, and 1-0.975^R = 0.049/0.073/0.119 for R = 2/3/5 are all correct. Pass-only-if-all-pass is correctly identified as an intersection-union test that needs no correction. Using alpha/n or Sidak for false-fail control of compatibility tests is right, the Bonferroni min(1,R*alpha) bound for dependent re-evaluations is right, the union bound gives sum alpha_r <= alpha for sequential rounds, power at the boundary is about alpha, and the three-region decision rule is sound. However: (1) the cross-round error control in Methods 2.4 item 5 and Core 7.1 is statistically wrong for confirmations whose pass means failing to reject compatibility, which covers performance estimates, data-driven measurements and method-independent agreement checks. (2) The threshold-validation carve-out in Methods 2.1 and Core 7.2 contradicts the requirement for method-independent confirmation of absolute-scale and performance claims on data. Several smaller wording inconsistencies follow.

findings.claim: Cross-round error control is defined only in terms of alpha as the false-pass rate, but it applies to every freeze. For confirmations where pass means failing to reject compatibility (closure, pull or stability validity checks under the tolerance rule; method-independent agreement for performance estimates and data-driven measurements), alpha is the false-fail rate and the false-pass rate is 1 - power. Option (a), sum alpha_r <= alpha, then makes each later round easier to pass. The statement that only (a) controls the overall false-pass rate at alpha is false for this class. Option (b)'s formula 1-(1-alpha)^R likewise does not bound false passes there. Repeated repair-and-reconfirm can therefore yield a T3-C 'confirmed' claim with an uncontrolled false-pass rate. Item 4 of the same section draws exactly this pass-versus-fail distinction for bins, but item 5 and Core 7.1 do not.
findings.element: Methods §2.4 item 5 (cross-round error control); Core §7.1 'Number of confirmation rounds'
findings.evidence_text: Counterexample: true bias 1 sigma. The per-round pass probability rises from 0.83 to 0.96 as alpha_r is halved, and P(pass within 4 rounds) is about 1.0 under a valid sum alpha_r = 0.025 allocation. Methods L214-L221 recognise that error type depends on which outcome is the rejection; L224 ignores this.

findings.claim: The two parts disagree on which confirmation a threshold claim on data needs. Methods L172 says absolute-scale or performance claims on data need method-independent confirmation; replacing it with a full systematic evaluation needs human approval, and otherwise the result is partial and 'not independently confirmed'. Methods L173 and Core §7.2 L509 say that applying a threshold directly to an untuned data-driven quantity is itself the confirmatory result, with no method-independent confirmation and no approval. Shared-systematic bias, which method-independent confirmation exists to catch, affects the threshold claim exactly as it affects the value. So reframing a performance claim on data as a threshold check bypasses the confirmation requirement. Core L510 also creates an asymmetry: the stronger claim (value +/- uncertainty) cannot reach T3-C without confirmation, while the weaker threshold claim on the same number can.
findings.element: Methods §2.1 'The claim type determines which type is needed' bullets 2-3; Core §7.2 T3-C threshold-validation row vs performance-estimate row
findings.evidence_text: Methods L172 vs L173; Core L509 vs L510. In practice the threshold carve-out is the 'replace confirmation with systematic evaluation' path (L232: systematics folded into the interval) that L172 makes conditional on human approval.

findings.claim: Core §7.1 gives only 1-(1-alpha)^R as the implied overall false-pass rate under option (b). It omits the Methods 2.4 condition that this holds only when every round uses an independent fresh sample, and that with any same-sample re-evaluation (which Methods L226 counts as a round) only min(1, R*alpha) can be reported. Read on its own, Core §7.1 would lead to understating the error rate.
findings.element: Core §7.1 'Number of confirmation rounds'
findings.evidence_text: Core L497 vs Methods L224 and L226.

findings.claim: Two rules contradict each other on low-sensitivity checks. Methods L202 says that when statistical sensitivity is insufficient, the result must be judged inconclusive. Methods L238-L239 says that a fail whose interval lies entirely outside the acceptance region is not changed because of insufficient power. A low-power check with the interval fully outside therefore gets inconclusive under L202 and fail under L239. L202 needs to be limited to the pre-execution sensitivity determination, or to the straddling case.
findings.element: Methods §2.3 four-valued result bullet 1 vs Methods §2.4 power rules
findings.evidence_text: L202 'statistical sensitivity is insufficient ... must be judged inconclusive' vs L239 'a fail in which the interval lies entirely outside the acceptance region is not changed because of insufficient power'.

findings.claim: The rules never say what a change of the derivation procedure made after seeing the derived value does to exposure. L160 asks only that it be recorded and that the difference be taken as a systematic or merely disclosed. The rules do not say that the quantity then counts as tuned or exposed, so it is unclear whether it loses the 'untuned, pre-declared procedure' status that L173 and Core L509 use to waive further confirmation. Taking the before/after difference as a systematic also does not remove the selection bias of a choice made because the value looked good.
findings.element: Methods §2.1 'Details of data-driven derivation' last bullet
findings.evidence_text: L151 (no exposure only if declared before looking), L160 (change after seeing: record and systematic or disclose), L173 (waiver for untuned pre-declared quantity), with no linking rule.

findings.claim: The power requirement has no stated target. The freeze table (L232) lists 'the a priori power design' without a target value.

answers.reasoning: Most of Methods §1 checks out physically. These parts are correct: the IOV/payload distinction, no silent fallback to 'latest', the covariance discipline, the four-layer association model, φ-symmetry constraining only intra-η-ring constants, the weak modes (twist/sagitta/telescope) not being visible to same-class split-sample residuals, the mass relation m = Z·R·√(1/β²−1) with δm/m ≈ γ²δβ/β ⊕ δR/R (I re-derived it: d ln m/dβ = −γ²/β), the exposure treatment of time-based, event-based and mixed exclusions, and the partition/RNG rules. The Control iteration rules (Control §1.1 families, §1.2 round changes, §4.2 non-final-round staleness, §4.6 labels, §4.7 iteration row) agree with Methods §1.6 and §4.4 for a simple chain of one attempt per round. There are two major defects. (1) The TPC/LArTPC/continuous-readout routing row defines t0 as per event (or per trigger). That is physically wrong for the cases the row names. With continuous readout, and in surface LArTPCs that see many cosmics in one drift window, t0 belongs to each interaction or track. The methods the row itself lists, such as cathode/anode crossing, give per-track t0. Under the rule as written, a single trigger t0 can be applied to out-of-time tracks, which gives wrong drift positions and wrong lifetime corrections. (2) Control requires exactly one step per round. It also marks as stale any consumer of a non-final round that lies outside the family. Together these rules cannot represent the typical partitioned calibration loop, where reconstruction with round-r constants is chunked over many attempts or steps (Methods §3) and then a global solve runs (mille→pede, φ-symmetry or π⁰ fits over the full sample). The per-chunk steps would be outside the family, so their consumption is stale. The only alternatives are an artificial single-attempt round, or hiding the loop inside one program, which escapes the §1.6 controls. Several minor wording and consistency problems are also listed.

evidence.requirement: case walkthrough or counterexample with locators

findings.claim: The TPC/LArTPC/continuous-readout row defines t0 as an offset per event (or per trigger). For continuous readout, and for LArTPCs with cosmic pileup inside the drift window, t0 is per interaction or track. As written, the rule permits one trigger t0 for all tracks, which gives wrong absolute drift positions and wrong drift-time-dependent attenuation corrections for out-of-time tracks.
findings.element: Methods §1.5 routing table, TPC/LArTPC/continuous readout row, 't0 is a time offset per event (or per trigger)'
findings.evidence_text: The same row lists cathode/anode crossings as a t0 source; these give per-track t0. The row's title includes continuous readout, where several collisions overlap in one drift time. The bold 'Without t0 ...' rule only governs the absence of t0, not the case of a t0 that is valid but wrongly assigned.

findings.claim: The Control iteration format (exactly one step per round, and staleness for any out-of-family consumer of a non-final round) cannot represent a partitioned calibration loop: chunked reconstruction with round-r constants followed by a global constant solve. Methods §1.6 and §4.4 claim to cover calibration/alignment loops, and Methods §3 requires partitioning for full-sample estimates.
findings.element: Control §1.1 families rule 'exactly one step per round'; Control §4.2 'u is a non-final round of an iteration and the consumer is not in the same family → stale'; Methods §1.6 'Each round is one step'
findings.evidence_text: An artifact is the output of one attempt (Control §4), so per-chunk refits must be separate attempts or steps. They cannot be family members because family/round allow only one step per round, so their consumption of round-r constants is stale. The only workarounds are a single attempt per round, which conflicts with Methods §3.1 and §3.2 scaling, or running the whole loop inside one program. The second puts the stopping rule in a content field that takes effect automatically, which bypasses the Methods §1.6 human approval for round and convergence changes. A design change is needed, e.g. allowing multiple steps per round or giving in-family sub-steps a round label.

findings.claim: The add-round path is underspecified. When a human approves extra rounds after non-convergence, the old final round keeps its required checks and its convergence fail unless the same contract also makes it unchecked. Otherwise it stays held, the new round's upstream stays waiting, and the new round is blocked_upstream indefinitely.
findings.element: Methods §1.6 add-round procedure; Control §1.2 family row; Control §4.7 iteration row
findings.evidence_text: Control §4.3: a fail leads to held. Control §4.2: bound requires ok, and d latest but not ok leads to waiting. Neither Methods §1.6 nor Control §4.7 says that the approved contract must demote round N to an unchecked intermediate round and move the two checks to round N+1.

findings.claim: The format does not require rounds to be chained. Control §4.2 lets any in-family consumer use any non-final round, so round r+1 need not consume round r (e.g. round 3 could consume round 1). This weakens the meaning of 'fed back' and of the convergence check.
findings.element: Control §1.1 families format rules; Control §4.2 in-family exemption; Methods §1.6 'do not invalidate the next round of the same loop'
findings.evidence_text: Methods L109 exempts only 'the next round'. Control L167 exempts any consumer 'in the same family', and L34 imposes no upstream requirement between consecutive rounds.

findings.claim: The family declares the convergence and unconstrained-mode checks by name, but required checks are a set of (check digest, criterion digest). The format rule 'the names of its required checks include these two checks' therefore has no defined matching. It is also unclear whether an approved replacement of one of these checks (a new digest) keeps the family valid.
findings.element: Control §1.1 families row and step specification 'required checks'
findings.evidence_text: L34 says 'convergence check name, unconstrained-mode check name' and 'names of its required checks'. L46 says required checks are a 'set of (check digest, criterion digest)'; no name field exists in the closed format.

findings.claim: Methods §1.6 says only changes to upstream or task-bound conditions invalidate results. Control §4.7 also lists program, environment and changes to the upstream list.
findings.element: Methods §1.6 bullet on criteria changes
findings.evidence_text: Methods L110: 'only changes to upstream or task-bound conditions invalidate results (Control §4.7)'. Control L229: 'upstream recomputed, or program, bound conditions, environment or upstream list changed → invalidated'.

findings.claim: Methods §1.8 requires a data/MC comparison giving a scale factor before any performance claim on data. Performance can be measured directly on data (e.g. tag-and-probe efficiency in data, or data-driven efficiencies without MC correction). A scale factor is needed only when MC-derived performance is transferred to data.
findings.element: Methods §1.8 second bullet
findings.evidence_text: The Methods §1.5 trigger row (L81) and Methods §2.1 (L151) accept data-driven measurements in data directly. L136 reads as making the SF format mandatory for every on-data performance claim.

answers.reasoning: Four requests were walked through Core §0.2-0.4, §5.1-5.4, §6.1-6.3 and §7.1-7.4, with the sections they route to in Methods, Control and Delivery. (1) T1 feasibility ('Can He isotope mass be reconstructed with TOF beta at high rigidity?'): the target tier is determinate (T1). The completion report is well defined (§7.2 T1 row, §7.4 T0/T1 column). However, the fast path (line 6) leaves out Core §5.2 and §5.3, and the T1 norms in them are not covered by its completeness justification (F2). (2) Simulated-sample performance number for internal use ('beta resolution on our MC'): determination rule 1 gives 'T2-numeric or T3-E' without saying how to choose, so the target tier is not determinate, and the choice changes which sections are loaded (VAL-01, Methods §2.1, exploratory marker) (F3). Otherwise the T2-numeric/T3-E path loads consistently: typical loading lists Control §0-8, Delivery §1.1 and §2.2-2.5; SCI-08 loads Methods §1.8. Core §5.4 maps to Control §7 without conflict, and the attested names in Core §7.4 paragraph 2 match Delivery §2.3. The Core §0.2 missing-part table, though, lets a T2-numeric deliverable be reported without the Methods part, which the trigger matrix requires for T2-numeric (F1, major). (3) T3-C performance estimate on flight data for a paper: rule 1 routes it to T3-C. VAL-01/03/04/06 and PROF-01 load Methods §2, §5 and Control §4.4. The freeze/confirmation/exposure rules agree across Core §5.4 items 4 and 7, Core §7.1-7.2, Methods §2.4, Control §1.1 'confirmation required', Control §4.4 and Control §7.2-7.3. The partial-completion rule for infeasible confirmation is consistent in Core §7.2, Control §1.1 and Methods §2.4 item 3. No contradiction was found on this path. (4) Implementation task ('fix BUG-03 in run_workflow.py' / 'implement C1'): the tier is T2-code. The 'Implementing layers B/C' row loads the whole Delivery part, plus the whole Control part when modifying C. Core §0.2's Control row and the T2-code typical-loading line say T2-code does not need / must not load the Control part, which can under-load a C1 task (F4). The T2-code contract-loosening approval in Core §6.1 and §0.4 item 10 is missing from the Core §6.3 human-decision table (F5). The completion report for T2-code is usable through the 'paragraphs that do not apply may be omitted' clause.

answers.reasoning: I read Control §2, §5.4, §5.5 and §7, Core §5.4 and the whole Delivery part closely, and checked them against the 0.49.1 snapshots. Most of the transition mapping matches the code. run_workflow records extension.argv with placeholders kept, script_sha256 only for .py tokens, versions.plugin_release, input_manifest with path and SHA-256, environment holding only python and numpy, exit_status, output_hashes, a top-level status list, and an artifact_id that is the same for every run of a step. TimeoutExpired is not caught, so a timeout leaves no run record. Absolute and '..' input paths are not blocked, and top-level inputs is []. The campaign has an intent/tag, unconfirmed/'intent' status, reconcile, confirm_submission, abandon_submission, not-submitted, lost, termination_observed, reset and resubmit as Delivery §3.1 describes. dependencies.py is advisory, and formal_use_allowed is always false. The hep-review CLI exposes operation-id append, checkpoint, export and import, with HeadMismatch/OperationConflict errors. Several rules still have no source in the code, or contradict another section. (1) A transition-period check-result is self-declared by the check program. Nothing binds its check digest, criterion digest or target digest to the program actually run, its declared inputs or the staged target, so a passing check can be attributed to a required check. (2) Some needed fields have no mapped source (the read list) or no defined serialization (the artifact-digest JSON). (3) The termination-certainty rule covers only the timeout case. Runs rejected before execution, steps skipped after an earlier failure, and the B1 termination flag are not covered. (4) Control §2 and Core §5.4 say the main Agent writes no receipt content, but Control §7.2 has it register termination certainty and usage. (5) Delivery §3.1 maps campaign states to reconcile and cancel-request in the transition period, which conflicts with Control §7.4 (no reconcile) and the Control §7.3 allowlist of line kinds. (6) Publish (Control §5.4) has no transition-period writer or line kind. (7) Admission before each step cannot be done inside a multi-step run_workflow invocation, and the hard 3600 s timeout conflicts with 'do not rely on timeout'. (8) Identity completeness does not cover a stale environment or code manifest, or an unknown plugin_release. (9) Core §5.4 item 1 says the run record replaces C's intent, while Control §2 and §7.1 say the registration line does. Finding F1 is major because it can let a check that should not count make an artifact ok. The others are local wording or consistency fixes.

evidence.requirement: conflict or gap list with locators

findings.claim: In the transition period, the identity of a check-result (check digest, criterion digest, target artifact digest, samples) comes only from the output file that the check program writes. No rule binds those digests to the check run's own run record: the check digest to argv/script_sha256 or the code manifest, the criterion digest to a criterion file in input_manifest, and the target digest to an artifact staged into that run's input_manifest. A trivially passing program can therefore write a required (check digest, criterion digest) and an arbitrary target digest, and Control §4.3 counts it as a pass of the required check. The attempt registration line identifies a check attempt only by 'output directory + step id' (step `__check__`), so it carries no declared check × criterion × target identity to compare against.
findings.element: Control §7.2 row 'check-result', together with the attempt-registration row; Core §5.4 item 2
findings.evidence_text: Control §7.2 L324: check-result = 'the output file of the check run (recording check, criterion, target artifact digest, four-valued result, samples), whose hash is in that check run's run record ... produced by the check program'. Control §4.3 L176: pass counts only when the check attempt 'has the identity this check × this criterion × this target'. Control §1.1 and Delivery §1.1 L33: the check digest is the check program digest. In code-run_workflow.py, record() (L132-143) stores argv, script_sha256 (only .py tokens, L116-124) and input_manifest, but nothing in the spec requires these to be compared with the self-declared digests. Delivery §5.1 L256 lists 'an unrelated attempt posing as a check' and 'a check that can only pass' as cases that must be rejected.

findings.claim: The Control §7.2 field mapping has no source for the intent's 'samples to be read' (the read list). Control §4.4 item 3, Control §5.1 item 3 and Control §2 (check-result samples 'must be in that check attempt's read list') need it. This contradicts the stated aim of §7 that 'every item of the derivation has a source'. In the transition period, a confirmation result's sample cannot be checked against a declared read list.
findings.element: Control §7.2 mapping table (missing row)
findings.evidence_text: Control §7 L304: 'so that every item of the derivation has a source and an order'. Control §2 L92 (intent: samples to be read) and L99 (samples used must be in the read list). Control §4.4 L187. The rows of Control §7.2 at L316-327 cover attempt, step, identity, consumed inputs, cost/usage, end status, termination, outputs, check-result, contract/freeze/exposure, decisions and session, but no read list. Core §5.4 item 7 L405 requires only that the freeze digest be cited in argv.

findings.claim: The artifact digest is defined as the SHA-256 of 'canonical JSON sorted by logical name', and the identity uses 'the SHA-256 of the input manifest', but neither serialization is fixed (separators, whitespace, encoding, non-ASCII escaping). The main Agent computes these digests by hand in the transition period, and C1 will compute them later. Different encoders give different digests, so consumed-input mappings and pins written now may not match after C1. The run record is written with indent=1, so it is not a usable canonical form either.
findings.element: Control §7.2 rows 'computational identity' and 'output and artifact digest'; Control §4 artifact definition
findings.evidence_text: Control §4 L153: 'canonical manifest of logical name → content digest (JSON with sorted keys)'. Control §7.2 L318 and L323. In code-run_workflow.py L262 the record is written with json.dumps(indent=1, sort_keys=True). DEC-01 (Delivery L226) covers the fact-log serialization, not the artifact-digest encoding.

findings.claim: The termination-certainty rule ('confirmed only if the run record exists ...; a timeout produces no run record ... unknown') covers only the timeout case. run_workflow also exits with no run record when the step was definitely not started: a missing input (exit 2), a failed parameter_digest command (exit 2), or a later step skipped after an earlier step failed. Read literally, a registered attempt becomes unknown and blocks its step until a human abandons it. Delivery §3.1 handles the analogous campaign case ('not-submitted') as a confirmed failure, so the treatment is inconsistent. The rule also ignores the B1 'termination: unconfirmed' flag: after B1, a run record can exist and still carry unconfirmed termination, and §7.2 would let the Agent register that as confirmed.
findings.element: Control §7.2 row 'termination certainty and order'
findings.evidence_text: Control §7.2 L322. code-run_workflow.py L205-209 (missing input: no record), L232-235 (parameter_digest failure: no record), L265-267 (break after a failure: later steps get no record). Delivery §3.1 L147 (not-submitted maps to a confirmed failure). Delivery §4.1 B1 L201 (termination flag). Core §5.4 item 3 L399 ('For gaps already fixed, citing their tests suffices').

findings.claim: Control §2 says the only loosening in the transition period is the registration lines, and that 'the main Agent still cannot write the content of a receipt'. Core §5.4 item 4 says the Agent 'does not write the contents of receipts'. Control §7.2 nevertheless has the main Agent write receipt fields: termination certainty (based on its own statement that no child processes remain) and resource usage. These are exactly the fields that decide attested (usage ≤ declared cost) and unknown versus terminal. The writer rule therefore contradicts the mapping. Either Control §2 and Core §5.4 must list these as further loosenings (and the report must label them), or the source must change.
findings.element: Control §2 transition bullet vs Control §7.2 rows 'declared cost and usage' and 'termination certainty'
findings.evidence_text: Control §2 L106: 'This is the only writer restriction loosened ...; the main Agent still cannot write the content of a receipt'. Core §5.4 item 4 L400. Control §7.2 L320: the Agent writes 'the actual usage ... in the run registration line'. L322: the run is registered as confirmed only if 'the main Agent has confirmed that there are no leftover child processes'. Control §2 L97: receipt fields include termination certainty and resource usage. Delivery §2.3 L91 (usage is part of attested).

findings.claim: Delivery §3.1 says the main Agent states the campaign-to-fact table in the transition period. That table includes 'reconcile after unknown' (job ended and result confirmed, confirm_submission followed by a later receipt or reconcile) and a 'cancel-request' fact. Control §7.4 says 'There is no reconcile in the transition period: an unknown attempt stays unknown ... until a human abandons it'. Control §7.3 limits the transition line kinds to contract, freeze, exposure, attempt registration, run registration, mapping table and transcribed decisions, so there is no line kind for cancel-request or reconcile. The two sections conflict. Under Control §7.4, a remote job whose ambiguous submission a person later confirms through the existing confirm_submission flow can never yield usable outputs. Delivery §3.1 also does not say that a campaign counts as an 'equivalent framework' that needs a Control §7.2-format field-mapping table (Control §7.1), which leaves its run-record fields without a source.
findings.element: Delivery §3.1 mapping table vs Control §7.4 first bullet and Control §7.3 line-kind allowlist
findings.evidence_text: Delivery §3.1 L136 ('stated by the main Agent according to the table during the transition period'), L143-144, L149. Control §7.4 L341. Control §7.3 L335. Control §7.1 L310. code-campaign.py confirm_submission L380-401 and docstring (an unconfirmed submission is settled by a person through reconcile and confirm_submission), poll: unknown is in POLL_AGAIN and may resolve later (L704-722).

findings.claim: The transition period has no path for publish. Control §5.4 requires publish per deliverable with compare-and-set on the derivation sequence number and a derivation version, and Control §2 makes C the only writer of publish. Control §7.3 does not list publish among the line kinds the main Agent may write, and Control §7 never says what replaces publish before C1, for example a statement in the completion report. Core §7.4 paragraph 1 still asks for 'deliverables already published'.
findings.element: Control §5.4 / Control §7.3 (missing transition handling)
findings.evidence_text: Control §5.4 L277. Control §2 L102 and L104 (publish written only by C). Control §7.3 L335 (allowlist without publish). Core §7.4 L527.

findings.claim: Control §7.1 and §7.2 require per-attempt admission and an attempt registration line before execution, a run registration line (the terminal fact) after execution, and an upstream that is usable (it has a producer with a terminal fact) at the downstream's admission (Control §5.1 item 4). run_workflow runs every step of a workflow back to back in one invocation and one work folder, with no point between steps where these lines can be written. In a multi-step invocation, the downstream's registration therefore precedes the upstream's terminal fact, and admission item 4 cannot be carried out as written. The spec never requires one step per invocation (one fresh output directory per step), which is the only arrangement under which the rules work.
findings.element: Control §7.1 admission bullet and Control §7.2 'attempt' and 'termination' rows vs run_workflow execution model
findings.evidence_text: Control §7.1 L309. Control §7.2 L316 and L322. Control §5.1 L260. code-run_workflow.py main() L203-267: a single loop over the topological order in one work folder. The tested shipped workflow runs three steps in one invocation (code-test_workflow_c6.py L36-40).

findings.claim: Core §5.4 item 3 says 'while BUG-04 is unfixed, do not rely on timeout'. run_workflow, however, imposes a fixed 3600 s timeout on every step and on the parameter_digest command, and the Agent cannot turn it off. Any step longer than one hour takes the BUG-04 path (no run record, unknown, human abandon), so it can never produce a usable artifact. The transition rules do not mention this limit or require such steps to be split.
findings.element: Core §5.4 item 3 (BUG-04 clause)
findings.evidence_text: Core §5.4 L399. code-run_workflow.py L48 STEP_TIMEOUT_S = 3600, used at L226-227 and L250 with no option to change it. Control §7.2 L322 (no run record means unknown).

findings.claim: The identity-completeness rule requires the code manifest and the environment_manifest.py output to be listed as step inputs, but never requires them to be produced or checked at execution time. environment_manifest.py record captures the environment of whichever process ran it, and a file staged from an earlier run hashes the same after the environment or code has changed. The 'identity' is therefore marked complete while not tracking the actual environment, and an artifact can be claimed current or reused across a real change. The rule also does not treat plugin_release with digest 'unknown' (INC-03) as an incomplete identity, even though the plugin modules imported by a step are then not identified.
findings.element: Control §7.2 row 'computational identity'; Core §5.4 item 4 'Identity must be complete'
findings.evidence_text: Control §7.2 L318. Core §5.4 L401. code-environment_manifest.py record() L109-122 (snapshot of the current process; a separate `check` subcommand L255-261 exists but is not required by the spec). code-run_workflow.py L151-153 (the digest may be 'unknown') and L116-124 (only .py tokens in argv are hashed).

findings.claim: Core §5.4 item 1 says that 'during the transition period the run record takes the place of the intent written by C'. Control §2 says the run records serve as the content of receipts and check-results, and that the main Agent's registration lines stand in place of C's intent. Control §7.1 requires both, the attempt registration line and the run record. The Core wording names the wrong stand-in for the intent.
findings.element: Core §5.4 item 1

Remote and campaign work in the transition period: is there a single consistent treatment of reconcile, cancel-request and confirm_submission across Control §7 and Delivery §3.1, including whether a campaign needs a Control §7.2 field-mapping table?

answers.reasoning: Most Control rules trace onto matching model code: closed format (validate_contract), strictness order (step_at_least_as_strict/contract_at_least_as_strict), effective contract, approval position and lapse (_contracts), single terminal fact (_exec), producer/owner/representative producer (producers/owner_step/best_producer), currency and upstream state (upstream_state), identity-bound holds (identity_failures/checks_state), freeze items 1-5 (freeze_ok), achieved tier, accepted, admission items 1-6, reuse, per-deliverable publish. Transition period and capability/permission matching are excluded with a stated reason (Control §8). The reference model runs clean (70/70 scenarios, 25/25 mutations killed). The attack scripts still found paths that use only permitted writes (contract, freeze, admission requests, publish), plus normal B receipts and check results: (1) a later contract that the spec treats as tightening adds a step with confirmation_required=false and allow_rerun=true. It takes effect automatically even under M2, after the human confirmed the first contract, and a T3C deliverable on that step is published with no confirmation sample and no human approval. Control §1.1 and §5.1 forbid this, while §1.2 and the model allow it. (2) The v12 rule against several copies and picking one (§5.1 item 6) can be bypassed with cosmetic content-field changes, which take effect automatically. Each change gives a fresh computational identity and a new draw, and the unchecked earlier copies leave no trace in prior_failures or in the publish fact. (3) In the model, an attempt id that admission already rejected can be admitted again. The intent is then ignored by _exec (state stays 'rejected'), so its cost escapes the budget and an unknown receipt on it does not block the same side effect. (4) Under M1 the claim that under-reporting cost cannot buy quota is false. (5) A test comment contradicts §1.1.

evidence.requirement: model run output or attack script result

findings.claim: A later contract that the spec counts as tightening can add a new step with confirmation_required=false and/or allow_rerun=true, plus a new T3C deliverable on it. It takes effect without a human, even under M2/M3 after the human confirmed the first contract, so 'deliverable reaches T3C' is published with no confirmation at all (and with copies picked by rerun). Control §1.1 (L53) allows 'no' only in the first contract or by human approval. Control §5.1 item 6 (L265) requires same-identity reruns to be 'stated in the first contract or approved by a human'. But §1.2 (L61, L67) checks only the steps of E and lets N add steps freely, and the model follows §1.2. The spec contradicts itself, and the model lets a confirmatory deliverable be accepted and published without the confirmation or the human approval that §1.1 requires.
findings.element: Control §1.2 strictness order (new steps unconstrained) vs §1.1 'confirmation required' and §5.1 item 6 allow_rerun; model contract_at_least_as_strict
findings.evidence_text: attacks.py a1_new_step_loosened_flags_m2: contract status 'effective'; DB achieved T3C, met True, 0 exposures of the confirmation sample; publish fact written with achieved T3C, prior_failures 0 (mode M2). Model L377-382 iterates only old['steps'].

findings.claim: The v12 fix in §5.1 item 6 claims that 'run several copies first, look at the outputs, and send only the one you like to be checked' is impossible, but it works per identity only. Program, environment and external dependencies are content fields that change automatically without approval (§1.2 L67). A cosmetic change (for example an external-dependency label) gives a fresh computational identity, so the agent can draw again, inspect, repeat, and check only the copy it likes. The earlier unchecked copies become 'invalidated' and leave no trace in the deliverable's historical failures or in the publish fact's failure count (§4.3 L179, §4.5 L201, §5.4). The same route turns a fail into 'another draw' with no real change to the computation, which item 6's first bullet ('what must change is the computation, not another draw') was meant to prevent. Closing this needs a design change, for example recording and publishing every superseded or invalidated output of the deliverable's step and its dependency chain, or not treating a content change as a new identity when it is unaccompanied by a reviewed computational change.
findings.element: Control §5.1 item 6 guarantee; §1.2 content fields change freely; §4.5/§5.4 history counts only fail/inconclusive
findings.evidence_text: attacks.py a2_cosmetic_content_redraw: same-identity copy rejected as designed; three recontracts changing only external=('note-k',) each 'effective'; X4 checked pass and published with prior_failures 0; earlier X1/X3 'invalidated' and unchecked.

findings.claim: In the model, an attempt id that admission rejected can be admitted again. Log._validate checks intent uniqueness only against earlier intents, so the second intent is accepted, but _exec keeps the state 'rejected' because 'intent' only moves the state from 'planned'. The admitted, executing attempt is then counted in neither in_flight nor used (budget bypass, contradicting §5.1 item 2). It is also excluded from same_identity_ran, and an unknown receipt on it does not block admissions with the same side effect (contradicting §3 'unknown' and §5.1 item 5). The spec says only 'attempt (unique)' for intents (§2 L92) and does not say whether rejected ids are reserved. Local fix: ids that appear in admission_rejected are unique too (or rejected admissions get no caller id).
findings.element: model Log._validate intent uniqueness (L131-134) and _exec state machine (L477-480); Control §2 intent 'attempt (unique)', §3, §5.1 items 2 and 5
findings.evidence_text: attacks.py a3: exec_status('z') == 'rejected' after a successful second admit; used+in_flight 1.0 instead of 2.0; after an unknown receipt on z, admit of z2 on the same step succeeds; committed cost 3.0 > budget 2.0. In a2, run 'x2' reused after a rejection silently produced no usable artifact.

findings.claim: §5.1 item 2 says without condition that 'under-reporting cost cannot buy quota', but receipt usage is mandatory only under M2/M3 (§2 L97, §4.1 L157). Under M1, when B reports no usage, the declared cost (which may be 0) is the whole charge and the output is still attested, so quota can be bought by declaring zero. The wording should be limited to M2/M3 or to receipts that carry usage.
findings.element: Control §5.1 item 2 wording vs M1 usage optionality; model charge/attested
findings.evidence_text: attacks.py a4: under M1 with budget 1.0, six attempts declared at cost 0 give used 0.0, and R1 is usable.

findings.claim: The model's t44 comment says that declaring confirmation-not-required in the first contract is allowed 'e.g. judged infeasible at freeze'. Control §1.1 says the opposite: an infeasibility determination at freeze does not change the contract, the field stays yes, and only a human may change it. The comment gives the wrong example.
findings.element: reference model t44 comment
findings.evidence_text: Model L1725 vs Control L53.

Can the 'no picking among copies' guarantee be stated and enforced across content-field changes (records of invalidated or unchecked copies on the dependency chain in the report and the publish fact)?
